pharm: Essential vitamin; cofactor for carbohydrate metabolism (pyruvate dehydrogenase, transketolase)
quick: Deficiency: 10-20 mg IM TID; Wernicke high-dose IV
summary: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is a water-soluble vitamin essential as a cofactor in carbohydrate metabolism. Parenteral thiamine is used to treat thiamine deficiency or beriberi (dry or wet) and is critical for Wernicke encephalopathy, infantile beriberi with acute collapse, and before/with IV dextrose in malnourished or alcohol-dependent patients. It is given IM or by slow IV when rapid restoration is needed, then continued orally to restore tissue stores.
indications: Thiamine deficiency and beriberi (dry and wet)
Cardiovascular disease due to thiamine deficiency (wet beriberi)
Neuritis of pregnancy when vomiting is severe
Prevention of Wernicke encephalopathy when giving IV dextrose to at-risk patients

dosage.n: Follow with oral multivitamin containing 5-10 mg thiamine daily for ~1 month

dosage.d: High-dose, e.g., 100 mg IV initially; guideline regimens use 200-500 mg IV three times daily
dosage.n: Give before/with IV glucose; high-dose per current guidelines

dosage.d: Administer slowly by IV route as an emergency cardiac measure
dosage.n: Risk of hypersensitivity with IV; see warnings

dosage.d: May respond to oral therapy; severe/collapse cases need parenteral
1-2 mg daily (RDA ~1.1-1.2 mg); higher for repletion

admin: Prefer IM or slow IV when rapid restoration is needed; oral for maintenance
Have resuscitation available for IV use due to rare anaphylaxis
In Wernicke or at-risk patients, give thiamine before or with IV glucose to avoid precipitating encephalopathy
Follow parenteral repletion with an oral multivitamin to saturate tissue stores
Consider an intradermal test dose in patients with suspected sensitivity
moa: Thiamine is converted to thiamine pyrophosphate, an essential coenzyme for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase, enabling oxidative carbohydrate metabolism and the pentose phosphate pathway; deficiency impairs energy metabolism, causing beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

relative: Prior reaction to parenteral thiamine (use cautious test dosing)
monitor: Signs of hypersensitivity during/after IV administration

preg: Considered safe at recommended intakes; requirements increase in pregnancy, and thiamine is used for neuritis of pregnancy with severe vomiting.
lact: Considered safe and recommended; thiamine is a normal milk constituent and lactating women have higher requirements.
renal: No specific dose adjustment; water-soluble vitamin readily excreted.

moderate: IV glucose/dextrose without thiamine — can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in deficient patients; give thiamine first
minor: Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide), long-term use — increase urinary thiamine loss
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; absorption is limited at very high oral doses.
interactions.alcohol: Chronic alcohol use impairs thiamine absorption and increases requirement; repletion is essential.
interactions.diagnostics: May interfere with some spectrophotometric uric acid and urobilinogen assays.

common: Transient warmth or local injection-site reaction
serious: Anaphylaxis / anaphylactoid reaction (mainly with repeated IV use)

monitoring: Watch for hypersensitivity, especially with IV dosing and repeated injections
Clinical response of neurologic and cardiac symptoms
Adequacy of oral repletion of tissue stores
counsel: Thiamine treats and prevents vitamin B1 deficiency
Tell staff if you have ever reacted to a thiamine injection
In alcohol dependence, regular thiamine helps prevent serious brain injury
Take oral supplements as directed to rebuild your body stores
Report rash, itching or trouble breathing after an injection
pk: Quick absorption; limited oral uptake at high doses
Biological turnover ~9-18 days for body stores
Protect from light; store per product labeling
pearls: In any malnourished or alcohol-dependent patient, give thiamine before or with IV glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy
Wernicke encephalopathy is treated with high-dose parenteral thiamine per current guidelines, not small oral doses
Rare but real anaphylaxis risk with IV thiamine — have resuscitation ready
Excess is renally excreted; toxicity from oral thiamine is essentially absent
Loop diuretics and chronic alcohol use increase thiamine loss/requirement
missed: Take a missed oral dose when remembered; skip if near the next dose. Do not double up. Parenteral repletion is scheduled by clinicians.
overdose: Oral thiamine has very low toxicity; excess is excreted renally. Large rapid IV doses may rarely cause anaphylactoid reactions — manage supportively with epinephrine and standard anaphylaxis care.
